records.name: Lampung
records.summary:
In November 2018, Satpol PP (the regional moral-and-order force) raided three transwomen in Lampung, an incident the comparative UNSW/Harvard review of violence against Indonesian transwomen records as police-perpetrated violence. Lampung is also among the eight provinces identified in OutRight's Creeping Criminalisation study as having discriminatory regional regulations. No further incidents, arrests, or enacted local bylaws specific to Lampung were found in the dossier period.

Deviation from the national score (0.15) is −0.02, at the minimum threshold. A single 2018 police raid on three transwomen is not a patterned campaign, and per the enforcement-over-statute rule, an OutRight-identified regulatory divergence without incident documentation is a small factor. The deviation is included because Lampung sits in the Sumatran belt where local Satpol PP enforcement against trans people is consolidating (alongside West Sumatra, South Sumatra, and North Sumatra).

Lampung is marginally above South Sumatra (0.13) in practical terms—both have one documented incident or announcement—but shares the same score due to equivalent evidence weight. It sits well above West Java (0.08), where a documented wave of ten attacks with 45 victims and zero prosecutions shows what unchecked local hostility looks like in operation.

freshness.fact: Same: national penal code effective Jan 2026 plus 2026 designation of 'LGBTQ+ culture spread' as a societal threat supersede the 2022 regional-drafting snapshot for this province.

records.name: West Papua
records.summary:
West Papua shares the same security-force pattern documented for Papua province: 138 recorded acts of torture or ill-treatment in detention by police and military (Sep 2021–Q1 2025) with near-total impunity, arbitrary airport detentions, expanded military deployments, and forced displacement through Q3 2025. No trans-specific incident series was identified. The risk to a trans visitor is amplification of any police contact into unlawful detention and physical violence at rates far exceeding the national norm.

Deviation from the national score (0.15) is −0.04. Like Papua, this is classified as a systemic-contact amplifier rather than a targeted-trans finding. The dossier explicitly notes the absence of trans-specific incidents while confirming that the probability of escalation during state contact is documented and elevated. West Papua's 2022 split from Papua means the same security apparatus operates under the same impunity conditions in the western portion of the island.

West Papua scores identically to Papua (0.11) and sits below the enacted-regulatory provinces West Sumatra (0.12) and South Sulawesi (0.12), where the risk is administrative or legislative rather than physical-state violence, and below Jakarta (0.12), where police overreach drew strong rights-group condemnation.

records.name: Central Kalimantan
records.summary:
Central Kalimantan is listed in the dossier among the provinces with no sub-national signal: no enacted discriminatory bylaw, raid, arrest or incident series targeting transgender people was found, and the province is NOT one of the eight identified in OutRight International's Creeping Criminalisation analysis of discriminatory regional regulations (that list covers Aceh, DKI Jakarta, East Kalimantan, Lampung, North Sumatra, South Sulawesi, South Sumatra and Yogyakarta).

For a visitor, Central Kalimantan therefore tracks the national baseline: the KUHP criminal code in force from 1 January 2026 criminalises same-sex conduct nationwide, and ordinary Sumatran/Java-style local moral policing is absent here — but there is no province-specific enforcement record in either direction. Any risk follows the country's national framework rather than a local divergence.

freshness.fact: 2022 regional-criminalisation landscape overtaken by the new national penal code in force Jan 2026 (cohabitation/extramarital acts), HRW World Report 2026 and a Jul 2026...

records.name: North Sumatra
records.summary:
North Sumatra is one of the eight provinces whose regional regulations OutRight's Creeping Criminalisation study examined as discriminatory toward women and LGBTIQ people, including rules touching sexual orientation and gender expression. No specific enforcement incident, police action, or enacted local bylaw targeting transgender people was documented in the dossier for this province. The signal is legal divergence without operational evidence.

Deviation from the national score (0.15) is −0.02, the minimum reporting threshold; the OutRight finding is a real but small factor absent enforcement documentation, and among the study's eight provinces the same no-incident profile appears in Yogyakarta.

For context, provinces with operational enforcement sit lower - Aceh (0.03) and West Java (0.08), and West Sumatra (0.11) with its enacted LGBT-targeting bylaws - while the capital territory, also an OutRight focus province, currently scores higher (0.16), and Bali 0.22. No sibling-specific violence or bylaw evidence elevates or depresses North Sumatra further.

records.name: North Sulawesi
records.summary:
OutRight's Creeping Criminalisation study examined regional regulations in eight provinces - Aceh, DKI Jakarta, East Kalimantan, Lampung, North Sumatra, South Sulawesi, South Sumatra and Yogyakarta - and North Sulawesi is not among them: the Sulawesi entry in the eight is South Sulawesi (the Makassar bylaw province), a different province. No enforcement incident, raid, arrest, or enacted anti-LGBT bylaw targeting transgender people was found in the dossier for North Sulawesi; the earlier attribution of an OutRight finding to this province was a misreading.

The recorded −0.02 deviation from the national score (0.15) was carried on that misattributed legal-divergence flag; the dossier contains no provincial evidence that would move North Sulawesi away from the national framework. A visitor-facing risk profile follows the national picture: the new KUHP code in force January 2026, and police extortion/arbitrary detention as the main mechanism.

North Sulawesi sits far above Aceh (0.03) and West Java (0.08), above West Sumatra (0.11), and below the capital territory (0.16) and Bali (0.22).

records.name: Southeast Sulawesi
records.summary:
OutRight's Creeping Criminalisation study analysed discriminatory regional regulations in eight provinces - Aceh, DKI Jakarta, East Kalimantan, Lampung, North Sumatra, South Sulawesi, South Sumatra and Yogyakarta. Southeast Sulawesi is not among them; the dossier records no specific enforcement incident, police action, or enacted bylaw targeting transgender people in this province, and its inclusion in an eight-province 'OutRight bloc' was a misattribution (South Sulawesi, a different province, is the Sulawesi entry in the study).

The −0.02 deviation from the national score (0.15) was recorded on the strength of the legal-divergence reading corrected above; on the dossier's evidence the province carries no provincial-level signal in either direction, and visitor risk follows the national framework.

Comparatively, Southeast Sulawesi sits above the violence/corporal-punishment and bylaw units (Aceh 0.03, West Java 0.08, West Sumatra 0.11) and below the capital territory (0.16) and Bali (0.22).

records.name: Special Region of Yogyakarta
records.summary:
Yogyakarta is among the eight provinces whose regional regulations OutRight's Creeping Criminalisation study examined as discriminatory, and is one of the eight (with North Sumatra) for which no specific enforcement incident, police action, or enacted anti-LGBT bylaw targeting transgender people was documented in the dossier. The signal is legal divergence without operational evidence. Despite its special administrative status and cultural prominence, no trans-specific incident was found; the OutRight finding confirms a regulatory layer but does not demonstrate enforcement against visitors.

Deviation from the national score (0.15) is −0.02, the minimum reporting threshold; Yogyakarta shares this minimal-divergence tier with North Sumatra.

It sits above the operational-enforcement provinces (Aceh 0.03, West Java 0.08, West Sumatra 0.11) where raids, corporal punishment or enacted bylaws exist, below the capital territory (0.16) - also an OutRight focus province - and below Bali (0.22), which has no documented regulatory signal and benefits from tourism-economy tolerance.

records.name: KwaZulu-Natal
records.summary:
KwaZulu-Natal is where documented street violence against queer people meets the country's most powerful traditional authority. A 2024 criminology study from a university in the province documents queerphobic violence and victimisation of self-identifying queer sexual minorities in KwaMashu, a township north of Durban — daily life in which the constitutional guarantee of equality does not reach. In January 2012 the Zulu King's anti-gay remarks at a harvest festival made the collision explicit: the royal house insisted the reported 'rotten' wording was a mistranslation; the South African Human Rights Commission said it would investigate; the provincial premier backed the royal family; and the Congress of Traditional Leaders of South Africa (CONTRALESA) responded that the Pietermaritzburg gay and lesbian network demanding an apology had shown the king 'disrespect' and was 'only seeking fame'.

For a discovered visitor, the province's pattern is that local moral authority — monarchy, chiefly councils, and the provincial government siding with them — has publicly ranged against queer claims, while academic documentation shows queerphobic violence persisting in its townships.
